subject: maths7
label: Maths
source: Topics from the test reminder on Arbor (7y/Ma1c, November 2026): place value, factors and multiples, order of operations, positive and negative numbers. Notes and questions are ours.

topics.title: Place value
topics.summary: What each digit is worth, multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1,000, comparing and ordering decimals, and rounding.
facts: Each column is worth **10 times** the column to its right. After the decimal point come **tenths**, **hundredths** and **thousandths**.
A **zero** holds a place: in 3,040,006 there are no hundred thousands, no thousands, no hundreds and no tens.
**× 10, 100, 1,000**: every digit moves **1, 2 or 3 places to the left**. **÷** moves them to the **right**. The decimal point stays still: 4.7 × 100 = 470, and 36 ÷ 1,000 = 0.036.
Multiplying by 10 does **not** just “add a zero”: 3.5 × 10 = 35, not 3.50.
**Comparing decimals**: line up the decimal points and compare from the left. Fill gaps with zeros: 0.4 = 0.40, which is bigger than 0.35.
**<** means “is less than”, **>** means “is greater than”: 0.62 > 0.618. The wide end faces the bigger number.
**Rounding**: look at the digit just **after** the place you are rounding to. **5 or more → round up**; 4 or less → it stays the same. 48,652 to the nearest thousand is 49,000.
**Decimal places (d.p.)** count the digits after the point. 7.963 to 1 d.p. is **8.0** — keep the zero, it shows the decimal place.
**Significant figures (s.f.)** count from the **first digit that isn’t zero**: 6,382 to 1 s.f. is 6,000; 0.0478 to 1 s.f. is 0.05.
A **billion** is a thousand million: 1,000,000,000.
keywords: one of the symbols 0–9 that make up a number
what a digit is worth because of the column it is in
a zero that keeps the other digits in the right columns
a column after the decimal point
a digit counted from the first non-zero digit
a whole number (it can be negative)

questions.stem: Write in figures: three million, forty thousand and six.
questions.explain: 3 millions, 0 hundred thousands, 4 ten thousands, then zeros in the thousands, hundreds and tens: 3,040,006.

questions.stem: What is the value of the 6 in 2.365?
questions.explain: The 6 is the second digit after the point — the hundredths column — so it is worth 0.06.

questions.stem: Write 0.7, 0.07 and 0.71 in order, smallest first.
questions.explain: Fill the gaps with zeros: 0.70, 0.07, 0.71. Now compare: 0.07 < 0.70 < 0.71.
Compare the tenths first: 0.5 has 5 tenths, 0.45 and 0.405 have only 4, and 0.09 has none.
3.4 = 3.40, and 40 hundredths is more than 38 hundredths. A longer decimal isn't always bigger.
True — 3 tenths is the same as 30 hundredths. A zero at the end after the point doesn't change the value.

questions.stem: 0.25 is bigger than 0.3, because 25 is bigger than 3.
questions.explain: False — compare the tenths: 0.3 has 3 tenths, 0.25 has only 2. So 0.3 = 0.30 is bigger than 0.25.

questions.stem: Which sign goes in the gap?  0.62 ___ 0.618
questions.explain: 0.62 = 0.620, and 620 thousandths is more than 618 thousandths, so 0.62 > 0.618.
× 100 moves every digit 2 places to the left: 4.7 → 470.
÷ 1,000 moves every digit 3 places to the right: 36 → 0.036.
The digit after the thousands is 6 (5 or more), so round up: 49,000.
The next digit is 6, so 7.9 rounds up to 8.0. Write 8.0, not 8 — the zero shows it's to 1 decimal place.
Look at the third decimal place: 1, so the 4 stays. 3.14.
The first significant figure is the 4 (the zeros before it don't count). The next digit is 7, so round up: 0.05.
The first significant figure is the 6 (thousands). The next digit is 3, so it stays: 6,000. Keep the zeros as placeholders.

questions.stem: A number line goes from 0 to 1 in 10 equal steps. What is each step worth?
questions.explain: 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1 — each step is one tenth.

questions.stem: How many hundredths are there in 0.4?
questions.explain: 0.4 = 0.40 = 40 hundredths.
A billion is a thousand million: 1,000,000,000. So two billion is 2,000,000,000 (nine zeros).

questions.stem: Multiplying by 10 always just adds a zero to the end.
questions.explain: False — it moves the digits one place left. 3.5 × 10 = 35, but “adding a zero” would give 3.50, which is still 3.5.

questions.stem: A whole number rounded to the nearest 10 is 70. What is the smallest it could be?
questions.explain: 65 rounds up to 70 (the 5 rounds up), but 64 rounds down to 60. So the smallest is 65.

topics.title: Factors and multiples
topics.summary: Factors, multiples, prime numbers, square and cube numbers, prime factors, HCF and LCM — and the word problems that use them.
facts: A **factor** divides into a number exactly. Find them in **pairs**: 12 = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4, so the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
A **multiple** is in the number's times table: multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, … — they go on for ever.
A **prime number** has **exactly two factors**: 1 and itself. **1 is not prime** (it has only one factor). **2 is the only even prime.**
Watch the traps that look prime: 51 = 3 × 17, 57 = 3 × 19, 91 = 7 × 13.
**Divisibility tests**: 2 — it's even; 3 — the digits add up to a multiple of 3; 5 — it ends in 0 or 5; 9 — the digits add up to a multiple of 9; 10 — it ends in 0.
**Square numbers**: 7² = 7 × 7 = 49. **Cube numbers**: 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. **Square root**: √49 = 7. **Cube root**: ∛64 = 4.
**Prime factors**: split the number in a **factor tree** until every branch ends in a prime: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = **2² × 3 × 5** (index form).
**HCF** (highest common factor): the biggest number that divides into both. **LCM** (lowest common multiple): the smallest number in both times tables.
**Venn diagram**: put the prime factors both numbers share in the middle. Middle multiplied = **HCF**; everything multiplied = **LCM**.
Word problems: “biggest possible equal groups / identical bags” → **HCF**. “When will they happen together again?” → **LCM**.
keywords: divides into a number with no remainder
a number in the times table
a number times itself three times (2³ = 8)

questions.stem: Write down the first five multiples of 7.
questions.explain: The 7 times table: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35. (1 and 7 are the factors of 7, not its multiples.)

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is prime: 21, 27, 29, 33?
questions.explain: 21 = 3 × 7, 27 = 3 × 9, 33 = 3 × 11. Only 29 has just two factors, 1 and 29.
False — a prime has exactly two factors. 1 has only one factor (itself).
False — 2 is prime (factors 1 and 2) and it is even. It's the only even prime.

questions.stem: Write down all the prime numbers between 20 and 40.
Write 36 as a product of its prime factors. Use index form.
questions.explain: 36 = 4 × 9 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 2² × 3². 4, 6 and 9 aren't prime, so keep splitting.

questions.stem: Write 84 as a product of its prime factors. Use index form.

questions.explain: Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. The biggest in both is 12.
Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. Multiples of 12: 12, 24. The first in both is 24. (96 = 8 × 12 is a common multiple, but not the lowest.)

questions.stem: Bus A leaves the bus station every 12 minutes and bus B every 15 minutes. They both leave at 9:00 am. When do they next leave together?
questions.explain: “Together again” → LCM. Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. Multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60. LCM = 60 minutes, so 10:00 am.

questions.stem: Ali has 24 apples and 32 pears. He packs them all into identical bags (each bag has the same fruit in it), using as many bags as possible. How many bags does he use?
questions.explain: “As many identical groups as possible” → HCF of 24 and 32 = 8. Each bag has 3 apples and 4 pears.
8 × 8 = 64, so √64 = 8. (Not 32 — that's halving.)

questions.stem: Which number between 50 and 100 is both a square number and a cube number?
questions.explain: 64 = 8² and 64 = 4³. 81 is square but not cube; 27 is cube but not square (and under 50).

questions.stem: Any whole number that ends in 5 is a multiple of 5.
questions.explain: True — multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5.
True — 4 + 7 + 1 = 12, and 12 is a multiple of 3. (471 = 3 × 157.)

questions.stem: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 and 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Use a Venn diagram to find the HCF of 60 and 72.
questions.explain: Shared prime factors (the middle of the Venn diagram): 2, 2 and 3. HCF = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.

questions.stem: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 and 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Use a Venn diagram to find the LCM of 60 and 72.
questions.explain: Multiply everything in the Venn diagram: 5 (only 60) × 2 × 2 × 3 (both) × 2 × 3 (only 72) = 360. (4,320 = 60 × 72 counts the shared ones twice.)
False — 91 = 7 × 13. It looks prime, but it isn't.

topics.title: Order of operations
topics.summary: BIDMAS: which part of a calculation to do first, working left to right, and putting brackets in to make a calculation true.

table.title: BIDMAS
head: Order
What
Example
rows: Division and Multiplication — equal, so left to right
Addition and Subtraction — equal, so left to right

facts: **BIDMAS**: **B**rackets, **I**ndices, **D**ivision and **M**ultiplication, **A**ddition and **S**ubtraction. (Some teachers say BODMAS — the O is for “orders”, the same as indices.)
Multiply before you add: 3 + 4 × 5 = 3 + 20 = **23**, not 35.
**× and ÷ are equal** — do them **left to right**: 24 ÷ 4 × 2 = 6 × 2 = **12** (not 24 ÷ 8 = 3).
**+ and − are equal** — do them **left to right**: 10 − 3 + 2 = **9** (not 10 − 5 = 5).
**Indices before ×**: 2 × 3² = 2 × 9 = **18**, not 6² = 36.
Work one step at a time and write each step on a new line — it's easier to spot a slip.
**Putting in brackets** to make a calculation true: try brackets round different pairs and work each one out until it gives the right answer.
Negative numbers follow the same order: −3 + 5 × 2 = −3 + 10 = **7**.
keywords: the order: Brackets, Indices, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction
how to work when the operations are equal

questions.explain: Multiply first: 3 × 4 = 12, then 5 + 12 = 17. (32 is what you get going left to right.)
Divide first: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, then 20 − 3 = 17.
Brackets first: 7 − 2 = 5, then 5 × 6 = 30.
Index first: 3² = 9, then 2 × 9 = 18. (36 would be (2 × 3)².)
÷ and × are equal, so left to right: 24 ÷ 4 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12.
− and + are equal, so left to right: 18 − 6 = 12, then 12 + 4 = 16.
Indices first: 16 + 9 = 25. (49 would be (4 + 3)².)
Both brackets first: 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
Brackets: 4 + 2 = 6. Index: 6² = 36. Then 3 × 36 = 108.

questions.stem: Put brackets in to make this true:  3 + 4 × 2 = 14
questions.explain: (3 + 4) × 2 = 7 × 2 = 14. Without brackets it would be 3 + 8 = 11.

questions.stem: Put brackets in to make this true:  20 − 8 − 2 = 14
questions.explain: 20 − (8 − 2) = 20 − 6 = 14. Left to right without brackets gives 20 − 8 − 2 = 10.

questions.stem: Put brackets in to make this true:  6 + 12 ÷ 3 + 3 = 8

questions.explain: False — multiply first: 2 × 3 = 6, then 8 − 6 = 2.
False — ÷ and × are equal, so left to right: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, then 5 × 5 = 25.

questions.stem: Sam says 6 + 4 × 3 = 30. What did Sam do wrong?
questions.explain: Sam did 6 + 4 = 10, then × 3. Multiply first: 4 × 3 = 12, then 6 + 12 = 18.
Multiply first: 5 × 2 = 10, then −3 + 10 = 7.
Index: 3² = 9. Multiply: 4 × 9 = 36. Then 50 − 36 = 14.
Brackets: 8. Index: 8² = 64. Then 64 ÷ 4 = 16.
Brackets: 2 + 4 = 6. Then left to right: 36 ÷ 6 = 6, and 6 × 3 = 18.

topics.title: Positive and negative numbers
topics.summary: Ordering negative numbers, the number line, temperature, and adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing with negatives.
facts: Negative numbers are **less than zero**. On a number line they are to the **left** of 0 (or below it, like a thermometer).
The further a negative number is from zero, the **smaller** it is: −8 < −3 (−8 °C is colder).
**Adding** a positive number: move **right** (up). **Subtracting** a positive number: move **left** (down). −4 + 9 = 5; 3 − 10 = −7.
**× and ÷**: **same signs → positive**, **different signs → negative**. Work out the numbers first, then decide the sign.
**Difference** between two temperatures: count the steps on the number line. From −9 °C to 14 °C: 9 up to 0, then 14 more = **23 degrees**.
**Halfway** between two numbers: add them and halve. Halfway between −8 and 2: (−8 + 2) ÷ 2 = **−3**.
Money below zero is a negative balance: £25 − £40 = **−£15** (overdrawn).
keywords: a number less than zero, written with a minus sign
a line with numbers in order, negatives to the left of 0
how far apart two numbers are

questions.stem: Put these numbers in order, smallest first:  3, −5, 0, −1, 2
questions.explain: On the number line from left to right: −5, −1, 0, 2, 3. −5 is further below zero than −1.
−8 is further below zero, so −8 °C is colder: −8 < −3.
Start at −4 and move 9 to the right: 4 steps gets you to 0, 5 more gets to 5.
Start at 3 and move 10 to the left: 3 to 0, then 7 more below zero = −7.
Start at −6 and move 5 further left: −11.
Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: 7 + 4 = 11.
Adding a negative is the same as subtracting: −2 − 6 = −8.
5 × 4 = 20. Different signs → negative: −20.
6 × 7 = 42. Same signs → positive: 42.
36 ÷ 4 = 9. Same signs → positive: 9.
(−3)² = −3 × −3. Same signs → positive: 9.

questions.stem: At midnight the temperature was −7 °C. By midday it had risen by 12 degrees. What was the temperature at midday?
questions.explain: −7 + 12: 7 up to 0, then 5 more = 5 °C.

questions.stem: The temperature in Oslo is −9 °C. In Rome it is 14 °C. What is the difference between the two temperatures?
questions.explain: From −9 up to 0 is 9 degrees, then 14 more: 9 + 14 = 23 degrees. A difference is never negative.

questions.stem: A submarine is at −120 m (120 m below the surface). It rises 45 m. What depth is it at now?
questions.explain: Rising means adding: −120 + 45 = −75 m, so it is 75 m below the surface.
False — −10 is further below zero, so −10 < −2.

questions.stem: Subtracting a negative number makes the answer bigger.
questions.explain: True — subtracting a negative is the same as adding: 5 − (−3) = 8.

questions.stem: What number is halfway between −8 and 2?
questions.explain: The gap from −8 to 2 is 10, half of that is 5, and −8 + 5 = −3. Or: (−8 + 2) ÷ 2 = −6 ÷ 2 = −3.
To go from −3 up to 4 you add 7. Subtracting −7 is the same as adding 7: −3 − (−7) = 4.
Left to right: −2 × 3 = −6, then −6 × −5 = 30 (same signs → positive).
Multiply first: 3 × −2 = −6. Then 4 − (−6) = 4 + 6 = 10.

questions.stem: A bank account has £25 in it. £40 is spent. What is the balance now?
questions.explain: 25 − 40 = −15, so the balance is −£15 (£15 overdrawn).
